judgments.label: uncertain
judgments.rationale: Teaser photo in the NEWS section, not inside a link: it sits in its own div and the headline link with the same text follows it in the same article. The crop shows a parked police car in livery on a street; the alt is the headline about a terrified woman trying to get out of a car during a chase, which the photo does not show, so the claim is true of the capture. My lean is that it fails 1.1.1: the alt conveys nothing of the photo and is not null either. But a concrete counter-reading holds up: the photo is a supplementary illustration of the adjacent headline (the WAI tutorial treats such eye-candy or adjacent-text images as decorative), and an alt that repeats the headline is a redundancy many auditors report as advisory rather than a 1.1.1 failure; no documented failure names a headline used as alt. Competent auditors would reasonably disagree, so uncertain. The live page (curl, 2026-11-21) has the same img, alt and markup, so the capture does not differ.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: Premium badge image before the Burglars headline. Its SVG (fetched live) draws the N hexagon logo and the word PREMIUM, and the screenshot shows 'N PREMIUM'; the alt is 'nottinghampost', the brand, so it does not convey the badge's information that the article is premium (paywalled). Nothing else in the teaser says Premium: the headline link's aria-label is the headline and the footer tag is Courts. The image is not decorative, since it is the only carrier of that status. I found no technique that makes it pass. The claim, read in good faith, says the alt names a label instead of what the image conveys, which is this defect. The live page serves the same img with alt 'nottinghampost'.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: Topic tag link 'Arnold' (aria-label Arnold, href all-about/arnold) in the footer of the teaser for the pub reopening story. The destination, fetched live, is the page titled 'Arnold news and views - NottinghamshireLive' with the h1 Arnold, so the link text is the name of the page it leads to, which describes its purpose (Understanding 2.4.4 accepts text that describes the purpose without the page's full name); the heading just before it is the story's headline, whose page is about an Arnold pub. The claim that the text does not tell where the link goes is false. Only one link named Arnold is in the snapshot, so R1 does not arise. Rampa did not read the destination, which is the context that settles it, so context_missing (it could also be read as a stricter rule than 2.4.4). The live page still has the link.
